  "claims": [
    {
      "id": "f1",
      "concept_id": "c1",
      "text": "sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) triggers checkpointing after a commit when a database on connection D has at least N WAL frames.",
      "source_id": "S3",
      "quote": "The sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) is a wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook() that causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f2",
      "concept_id": "c1",
      "text": "Each new connection enables auto-checkpointing at a default threshold of 1000 pages or the SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT setting.",
      "source_id": "S3",
      "quote": "Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f3",
      "concept_id": "c1",
      "text": "Passing N equal to zero or a negative value to sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() disables automatic checkpoints.",
      "source_id": "S3",
      "quote": "Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f4",
      "concept_id": "c2",
      "text": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE checkpoints available frames without waiting for database readers or writers to finish.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f5",
      "concept_id": "c2",
      "text": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE never invokes the busy-handler callback.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode. On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished if there are concurrent readers or writers.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f6",
      "concept_id": "c2",
      "text": "Automatic checkpoints use PASSIVE mode.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "All checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and by the automatic checkpoint mechanism are PASSIVE.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f7",
      "concept_id": "c3",
      "text": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL waits until there is no writer and all readers use the most recent snapshot, then checkpoints all frames and syncs the database.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot. It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f8",
      "concept_id": "c3",
      "text": "A pending SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL blocks new writers while allowing new readers.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f9",
      "concept_id": "c4",
      "text": "Checkpoint copying must stop when it reaches a WAL page beyond any current reader's end mark.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f10",
      "concept_id": "c4",
      "text": "If overlapping read transactions always keep a reader active, checkpoints cannot complete and the WAL can grow without bound.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f11",
      "concept_id": "c4",
      "text": "Attempting checkpoints during reader gaps, when no process reads the database, avoids continuous-reader checkpoint starvation.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are \"reader gaps\": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f12",
      "concept_id": "c5",
      "text": "If another process holds the checkpoint lock, the checkpoint call returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the busy handler.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f13",
      "concept_id": "c5",
      "text": "If the busy handler returns 0 before acquiring the writer lock or while waiting for readers, the checkpoint falls back to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE behavior.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f14",
      "concept_id": "c5",
      "text": "The fallback to partial, nonblocking checkpoint work after a busy-handler abort still returns SQLITE_BUSY.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f15",
      "concept_id": "c6",
      "text": "COMMIT operations that trigger automatic checkpointing can be much slower than ordinary COMMIT operations.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "This has the effect of causing most COMMIT operations to be very fast but an occasional COMMIT (those that trigger a checkpoint) to be much slower.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f16",
      "concept_id": "c6",
      "text": "With PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL, running checkpoints in a separate thread or process prevents the query/update thread or process from blocking on sync operations.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "If an application therefore runs checkpoint in a separate thread or process, the main thread or process that is doing database queries and updates will never block on a sync operation.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f17",
      "concept_id": "c7",
      "text": "Regular checkpoints keep the WAL small to maintain read performance.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "Hence, to maintain good read performance it is important to keep the WAL file size down by running checkpoints at regular intervals.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f18",
      "concept_id": "c7",
      "text": "Less frequent checkpointing amortizes each checkpoint's cost across more writes.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "To maximize write performance, one wants to amortize the cost of each checkpoint over as many writes as possible, meaning that one wants to run checkpoints infrequently",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f19",
      "concept_id": "c8",
      "text": "Crash-safe checkpointing requires WAL sync before copying into the database and database-file sync before WAL reset.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f20",
      "concept_id": "c9",
      "text": "A reader's fixed WAL end mark gives its read transaction a single point-in-time snapshot.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "But for any particular reader, the end mark is unchanged for the duration of the transaction, thus ensuring that a single read transaction only sees the database content as it existed at a single point in time.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f21",
      "concept_id": "c10",
      "text": "After checkpointing, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART waits until every reader uses only the database file, ensuring that the next writer restarts the WAL from its beginning.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback ) until all readers are reading from the database file only. This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f22",
      "concept_id": "c11",
      "text": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE adds truncation to zero bytes immediately before successful return to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART behavior.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f23",
      "concept_id": "c12",
      "text": "With PRAGMA synchronous=FULL, writers sync the WAL at every transaction commit.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "(Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL but omit this sync if PRAGMA synchronous is set to NORMAL.)",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f24",
      "concept_id": "c12",
      "text": "Under PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL, checkpointing is the only operation that issues an I/O barrier or sync.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation (fsync() on unix or FlushFileBuffers() on windows).",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f25",
      "concept_id": "c12",
      "text": "Omitting WAL disk sync sacrifices durability after power loss or hard reboot.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "Further, syncing the content to the disk is not required, as long as the application is willing to sacrifice durability following a power loss or hard reboot.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f26",
      "concept_id": "c13",
      "text": "When pnLog is non-NULL, *pnLog reports total WAL frames, or -1 if an error or non-WAL database prevents checkpointing.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "*pnLog is set to the total number of frames in the log file or to -1 if the checkpoint could not run because of an error or because the database is not in WAL mode .",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f27",
      "concept_id": "c13",
      "text": "*pnCkpt counts checkpointed frames in the current WAL, including frames checkpointed before the current call.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "*pnCkpt is set to the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called)",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f28",
      "concept_id": "c14",
      "text": "Installing the sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() callback replaces any existing sqlite3_wal_hook() callback.",
      "source_id": "S3",
      "quote": "The callback registered by this function replaces any existing callback registered using sqlite3_wal_hook() .",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f29",
      "concept_id": "c14",
      "text": "Registering sqlite3_wal_hook() disables automatic checkpointing configured through sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint().",
      "source_id": "S3",
      "quote": "Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f30",
      "concept_id": "c15",
      "text": "On a write, SQLite can rewind the WAL when it has been fully transferred into the database and synced and no readers still use it.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f31",
      "concept_id": "c15",
      "text": "Ordinary checkpoint recycling reuses the WAL file by overwriting from its beginning rather than normally truncating it.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f32",
      "concept_id": "c16",
      "text": "The shared-memory wal-index prevents SQLite WAL from working on a network filesystem.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "The wal-index greatly improves the performance of readers, but the use of shared memory means that all readers must exist on the same machine. This is why the write-ahead log implementation will not work on a network filesystem.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f33",
      "concept_id": "c17",
      "text": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP exposes the WAL-frame and checkpointed-frame counters while checkpointing zero frames.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f34",
      "concept_id": "c18",
      "text": "A large write transaction can grow the WAL because WAL reset cannot occur during the transaction.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction. So a large change to a large database might result in a large WAL file.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f35",
      "concept_id": "c19",
      "text": "Rollback-journal recovery restores original database content by replaying the journal after a crash or ROLLBACK.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "In the event of a crash or ROLLBACK , the original content contained in the rollback journal is played back into the database file to revert the database file to its original state.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f36",
      "concept_id": "c20",
      "text": "When zDb is NULL or empty, an all-attached-WAL checkpoint call leaves *pnLog and *pnCkpt undefined.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "zDb is NULL or points to a zero length string, then the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db. In this case the values written to output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt are undefined.",
      "pass": 0
    }
  ],

    {
      "pass": 0,

      "total_claims": 36,
      "new_information_rate": 1.0
    }
  ],

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) triggers checkpointing after a commit when a database on connection D has at least N WAL frames.
claims.quote: The sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) is a wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook() that causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: Each new connection enables auto-checkpointing at a default threshold of 1000 pages or the SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT setting.
claims.quote: Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.

claims.text: Passing N equal to zero or a negative value to sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() disables automatic checkpoints.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE checkpoints available frames without waiting for database readers or writers to finish.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE never invokes the busy-handler callback.
claims.quote: The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode. On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished if there are concurrent readers or writers.

claims.text: Automatic checkpoints use PASSIVE mode.
claims.quote: All checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and by the automatic checkpoint mechanism are PASSIVE.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL waits until there is no writer and all readers use the most recent snapshot, then checkpoints all frames and syncs the database.
claims.quote: This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot. It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file.

claims.text: A pending SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL blocks new writers while allowing new readers.
claims.quote: This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

claims.text: Checkpoint copying must stop when it reaches a WAL page beyond any current reader's end mark.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: If overlapping read transactions always keep a reader active, checkpoints cannot complete and the WAL can grow without bound.
claims.quote: However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: Attempting checkpoints during reader gaps, when no process reads the database, avoids continuous-reader checkpoint starvation.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: If another process holds the checkpoint lock, the checkpoint call returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the busy handler.
claims.quote: If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.

claims.text: If the busy handler returns 0 before acquiring the writer lock or while waiting for readers, the checkpoint falls back to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE behavior.
claims.quote: If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE

claims.text: The fallback to partial, nonblocking checkpoint work after a busy-handler abort still returns SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.

claims.text: COMMIT operations that trigger automatic checkpointing can be much slower than ordinary COMMIT operations.
claims.quote: This has the effect of causing most COMMIT operations to be very fast but an occasional COMMIT (those that trigger a checkpoint) to be much slower.

claims.text: With PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL, running checkpoints in a separate thread or process prevents the query/update thread or process from blocking on sync operations.
claims.quote: If an application therefore runs checkpoint in a separate thread or process, the main thread or process that is doing database queries and updates will never block on a sync operation.

claims.text: Regular checkpoints keep the WAL small to maintain read performance.
claims.quote: Hence, to maintain good read performance it is important to keep the WAL file size down by running checkpoints at regular intervals.

claims.text: Less frequent checkpointing amortizes each checkpoint's cost across more writes.
claims.quote: To maximize write performance, one wants to amortize the cost of each checkpoint over as many writes as possible, meaning that one wants to run checkpoints infrequently

claims.text: Crash-safe checkpointing requires WAL sync before copying into the database and database-file sync before WAL reset.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: A reader's fixed WAL end mark gives its read transaction a single point-in-time snapshot.
claims.quote: But for any particular reader, the end mark is unchanged for the duration of the transaction, thus ensuring that a single read transaction only sees the database content as it existed at a single point in time.

claims.text: After checkpointing, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART waits until every reader uses only the database file, ensuring that the next writer restarts the WAL from its beginning.
claims.quote: after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback ) until all readers are reading from the database file only. This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE adds truncation to zero bytes immediately before successful return to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART behavior.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: With PRAGMA synchronous=FULL, writers sync the WAL at every transaction commit.
claims.quote: (Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL but omit this sync if PRAGMA synchronous is set to NORMAL.)

claims.text: Under PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL, checkpointing is the only operation that issues an I/O barrier or sync.
claims.quote: Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation (fsync() on unix or FlushFileBuffers() on windows).

claims.text: Omitting WAL disk sync sacrifices durability after power loss or hard reboot.
claims.quote: Further, syncing the content to the disk is not required, as long as the application is willing to sacrifice durability following a power loss or hard reboot.

claims.text: When pnLog is non-NULL, *pnLog reports total WAL frames, or -1 if an error or non-WAL database prevents checkpointing.
claims.quote: *pnLog is set to the total number of frames in the log file or to -1 if the checkpoint could not run because of an error or because the database is not in WAL mode .

claims.text: *pnCkpt counts checkpointed frames in the current WAL, including frames checkpointed before the current call.
claims.quote: *pnCkpt is set to the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called)

claims.text: Installing the sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() callback replaces any existing sqlite3_wal_hook() callback.
claims.quote: The callback registered by this function replaces any existing callback registered using sqlite3_wal_hook() .

claims.text: Registering sqlite3_wal_hook() disables automatic checkpointing configured through sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint().
claims.quote: Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.

claims.text: On a write, SQLite can rewind the WAL when it has been fully transferred into the database and synced and no readers still use it.
claims.quote: if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning

claims.text: Ordinary checkpoint recycling reuses the WAL file by overwriting from its beginning rather than normally truncating it.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

claims.text: The shared-memory wal-index prevents SQLite WAL from working on a network filesystem.
claims.quote: The wal-index greatly improves the performance of readers, but the use of shared memory means that all readers must exist on the same machine. This is why the write-ahead log implementation will not work on a network filesystem.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP exposes the WAL-frame and checkpointed-frame counters while checkpointing zero frames.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: A large write transaction can grow the WAL because WAL reset cannot occur during the transaction.
claims.quote: the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction. So a large change to a large database might result in a large WAL file.

claims.text: Rollback-journal recovery restores original database content by replaying the journal after a crash or ROLLBACK.
claims.quote: In the event of a crash or ROLLBACK , the original content contained in the rollback journal is played back into the database file to revert the database file to its original state.

claims.text: When zDb is NULL or empty, an all-attached-WAL checkpoint call leaves *pnLog and *pnCkpt undefined.
claims.quote: zDb is NULL or points to a zero length string, then the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db. In this case the values written to output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt are undefined.
